issues.legal_issue: Profits from selling chemicals and raw materials as part of a winding-up realisation sale are not taxable as profits from trading when the sale is not part of an ongoing trading business.
material_facts: The company had stopped manufacturing matches after its profits declined and sold the factory assets to end that business.

A later agreement included chemicals and paper for manufacture that had been excluded from the initial agreement, but no separate price for those items was identified; the consideration was a single increased price.
The factory continued to operate after the sale agreement only on behalf of the purchaser while the consideration was being paid.
Before the sale, the company had made only two small sales of chemicals, which did not show continued or sustained trading in chemicals.
Although the company’s memorandum authorised it to manufacture and sell chemicals, the evidence showed that this authority had not been used as an ongoing business.
issues.conclusion: The sale of the chemicals and raw materials was part of a winding-up sale to realise the company’s assets, not a sale in the course of business operations. The assessed profit was therefore not liable to income tax, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A mere realisation of assets in winding up is not trading; tax on a profit requires that the profit arise from trading or business operations. Whether a sale during a business’s closure is trading depends on the acts actually undertaken and the circumstances of the sale, not merely the taxpayer’s intention or its authority under its memorandum. A slump sale with no identifiable price attributable to stock does not, on that fact alone, establish a taxable trading profit. The Court relied principally on Doughty v Commissioner of Taxes (1927) A.C. 327, which distinguishes a winding-up sale from a sale made as part of trading, and considered Californian Copper Syndicate v Harris (1904) 5 T.C. 159, Tebrau (Johore) Rubber Syndicate Ltd. v Farmer (1910) 5 T.C. 658, Commissioner of Taxation (W.A.) v Newman (1921) 29 C.L.R. 484, Anson v Commissioner of Taxes (1922) N.Z.L.R. 330, J. & R. O’Kane & Co. v Commissioners of Inland Revenue (1922) 12 T.C. 303, The Commissioner of Inland Revenue v “Old Bashmills” Distillery Co. Ltd. (in Liquidation) (1926) 12 T.C. 1148, and J. and M. Craig (Kilmarnock), Ltd. v Cowperthwaite (1914) 13 T.C. 627. Section 25 of the Travancore Income-tax Act was the basis for the notice concerning escaped assessment; the judgment did not identify it as the substantive test for whether the sale profit was taxable.

rule.if: income_tax_appeal and sale_to_close_business and buyer_operated_factory_for_its_own_account and only_trivial_prior_chemical_sales and unallocated_slump_price

predicates.income_tax_appeal: The dispute came before the court in an appeal concerning an income-tax assessment on profit alleged to have escaped assessment.
predicates.sale_to_close_business: The company sold its factory assets and associated materials as part of ending its manufacturing business.
predicates.buyer_operated_factory_for_its_own_accou: After the sale agreement, the company kept the factory operating on behalf of the purchaser rather than for its own business.
predicates.only_trivial_prior_chemical_sales: Before the sale, the company had made only two small sales of chemicals, which did not evidence sustained trading in chemicals.
predicates.unallocated_slump_price: The agreement set a single price for the assets and materials without identifying a separate amount for the chemicals and raw materials.

issues.definition: When an income-tax appeal concerns a sale to close a business, and the buyer operated the factory for its own account, prior chemical sales were only trivial, and the slump price was unallocated, the profit is treated as a non-taxable winding-up realisation rather than business income.
